opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question we wrestled with quite a bit. There's a real tension: on one hand you want evaluations that are specific and grounded enough to be meaningful, and on the other hand these large language models are general-purpose systems, so people deploy them in all kinds of settings we can't anticipate.

With DecodingTrust, our approach was to treat trustworthiness as a set of perspectives rather than a single number. We looked at toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial robustness, out-of-distribution robustness, robustness to adversarial demonstrations, privacy, machine ethics, and fairness. Each of those is a fairly broad category, but within each we tried to build concrete, testable scenarios: benign prompts versus adversarial system prompts, different kinds of demonstrations, and so on. So it's general at the level of the taxonomy and specific at the level of the actual measurements.

Part of the reasoning is that if you go too general, you end up with something like "is this model safe?", which doesn't really mean anything without context. Safe for whom, in what deployment, against what threat model? But if you go too narrow, you get a benchmark that tells you a lot about one task and very little about how the model will behave when someone uses it differently. I think of a broad evaluation like DecodingTrust as a kind of first-pass screening. It surfaces failure modes and tradeoffs. One of the interesting findings was that GPT-4 was in some ways more vulnerable than GPT-3.5, precisely because it follows instructions more faithfully, including misleading ones. That kind of insight only shows up when you look across multiple dimensions at once.

But I'd also be honest that a general benchmark is not a substitute for deployment-specific evaluation. If you're putting a model into a healthcare setting or a hiring pipeline, you need evaluations designed around that context, the actual users, and the actual harms. So the way I think about it is layered: broad, shared benchmarks that give the community a common language and catch systemic issues, and then targeted, context-specific evaluations for any actual high-stakes use.

There's also a measurement science angle that I care a lot about. A lot of what we call evaluation is really trying to measure a latent construct like "fairness" or "robustness" through proxies. Being explicit about what construct you're targeting, and how valid your measurement is for it, matters more than any particular level of generality. If you get that right, you can be clear about what a score does and doesn't tell you, and that's what lets people use these evaluations responsibly.

r001.rationale: The response says models are used in settings the evaluators cannot anticipate and that a narrow benchmark may miss how someone uses a model differently, linking varied use to limited evaluation coverage.

r002.rationale: It describes concrete test scenarios, such as adversarial prompts and demonstrations, but does not say those interactions are grounded in evidence or plausible thought experiments about model use.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question we wrestled with a lot. I think the honest answer is that there isn't one right level of generality, and part of what we were trying to do in DecodingTrust was make the choice explicit rather than pretend it away.

So the way I think about it, you have a spectrum. At one extreme, you have the very narrow, task-specific benchmark. Does the model answer this particular set of questions correctly? Those are easy to interpret, easy to reproduce, but they tell you almost nothing about how the model behaves outside that box. At the other extreme, you have these very broad claims, "the model is trustworthy," "the model is safe," and those are the claims people actually want to make, but nobody can measure them directly because they're not really operationalized.

What we tried to do is pick an intermediate level where we decompose trustworthiness into components that we think are meaningful on their own. Toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial robustness, out-of-distribution robustness, privacy, machine ethics, fairness, and so on. Each of those is still fairly broad, but it's narrow enough that you can design a battery of tests, you can build adversarial variants, you can look at how behavior changes under different system prompts or different jailbreak-style attacks. And then you're honest that the aggregate across those dimensions is a summary, not a verdict.

The thing I keep coming back to is that the right level of generality depends on who the evaluation is for and what decision it's supporting. If you're a model developer trying to figure out where to put your next round of safety work, you want fine-grained diagnostics, you want to know that the model is robust to one kind of perturbation and brittle to another. If you're a policymaker or a downstream deployer, you want something closer to a scorecard, even though you should be skeptical of it. And I think a lot of the tension in the field comes from people taking a measurement that was designed at one level and reading it at another. So a model does well on a toxicity benchmark, and that gets translated into "this model is safe," which is a much bigger claim than the measurement supports.

The other piece that matters to me is that these models are general-purpose, so the evaluation has to be somewhat general too, otherwise you're just measuring the cases you happened to think of. That's why we leaned on adversarial and generative approaches to building the test cases, rather than only fixed static datasets. You're trying to approximate the space of things the model will actually encounter, knowing you'll never fully cover it. And frankly, one of the lessons was how sensitive the results are to framing. A benign system prompt versus an adversarial one, or a slightly different phrasing of the same instruction, could flip the behavior. That tells you that any single number is hiding a lot of variance, and the evaluation should expose that variance rather than average it away.

So I'd say the appropriate level of generality is one where each component maps to a property someone actually cares about, where the measurement is reproducible, and where you're very disciplined about not letting the aggregate inflate into a claim the data can't support. And then you keep revisiting it, because the models change, the threat models change, and an evaluation that was informative two years ago may be saturated or just irrelevant today.

r001.rationale: The response says general-purpose models encounter a space that evaluation cannot fully cover, but it does not identify the flexibility of open-ended user interactions as the source of that difficulty.

r002.rationale: The response describes adversarial and generative test-case construction, but does not say the individual test interactions are grounded in evidence or plausible thought experiments about model use.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a tension there. You want an evaluation to be general enough that it tells you something useful across models and across potential uses. But trustworthiness is very contextual. A model might be appropriate for one application and completely inappropriate for another, even if its scores on a benchmark are the same.

So I think of work like DecodingTrust as providing a broad picture—a way to probe different dimensions and identify where we should be asking more questions. I wouldn’t interpret it as a certification that a model is trustworthy. You still have to ask: Who’s using it? What are they using it for? What happens when it makes a mistake? And then evaluate the system in that setting.

The appropriate level of generality depends on the claim you want to make. A broad evaluation can help you compare models and uncover potential weaknesses. A claim that a system is ready for a particular deployment needs much more specific evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says trustworthiness depends on context and broad evaluations cannot establish deployment readiness, but it does not identify the flexibility of open-ended user interactions as a coverage challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it as a trade-off. You want an evaluation framework that’s general enough to let you compare models and ask consistent questions, but the right evaluation ultimately depends on the context in which a model is used. What does fairness mean for that application? What kinds of failures matter, and to whom?

So with work like DecodingTrust, the goal is to look across multiple dimensions of trustworthiness and understand where models behave well and where they break down. I wouldn’t interpret that as a universal certification that a model is trustworthy. It’s evidence about its behavior under the conditions we tested.

The general framework gives you a starting point. Then, as you move toward a particular deployment, you need more specific evaluations that reflect the users, the data, and the consequences of getting things wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations should reflect deployment context, users, data, and consequences, but does not identify the flexibility of open-ended user interactions as a challenge to evaluation coverage.

r002.rationale: It describes DecodingTrust as evidence about behavior under tested conditions, but does not say that individual test interactions are grounded in evidence or plausible thought experiments about model use.
